html:
Muscat is a port on the Gulf of Oman, and on the map its name stands for the Omani coast from about 1000 to 1500. It lies near the Strait of Hormuz, the narrow mouth of the Persian Gulf, and has been a trading port since at least the 1st century CE.

In these centuries Oman had two faces. Inland, in the valleys of the Hajar Mountains, the Ibadi Muslims chose imams to lead them, a form of Islam that survives today mainly in Oman. On the coast, ports like Sohar, Qalhat and Muscat lived from the sea. Ships carried horses, dates and frankincense to India and brought back cloth, spices and timber, part of the Indian Ocean trade that linked East Africa, Arabia, Persia and India.

Outside powers came and went. Persian dynasties such as the Buyids and later the Seljuks held the coast at times. From the 1100s the local Nabhani kings ruled parts of Oman. In the 1300s and 1400s the island trading state of Hormuz controlled much of the Gulf trade, and Qalhat and Muscat paid it tribute.

The period ends with the Portuguese. In 1507 Afonso de Albuquerque attacked the Omani ports and took Muscat, which Portugal held as a fort on its sea route to India until Omanis drove it out in 1650. After that Muscat became the capital of an Omani sea power that reached as far as Zanzibar, and later of Muscat and Oman.
